$comment: Three tiers, from GDD section 2.2. These are renderings, not creatures: hostile code manifests as a goblin the way a file manifests as an icon. That is what keeps the setting a corporate dystopia rather than a fantasy world, and it makes threat legible at a glance - seeing a Minotaur tells the player the difficulty changed without a number appearing anywhere. Scarcity is the tuning knob.
$stats_comment: Tier identity and meaning are canon. Health, damage and speed are INFERRED - canon does not specify combat numbers. Enemies drop nothing: materials come from the world, and drop tables would make fighting a gathering strategy, which inverts the loop.

tiers.name: Goblin
tiers.represents: Baseline firewalls and low-skill rival hackers
tiers.description: The system's cheapest answer to an intruder. Arrives in numbers because it is not worth anything individually.

tiers.name: Minotaur
tiers.represents: Hardened defences and genuinely competent rivals
tiers.description: Something in the program decided you were worth spending on. Only ever a few.

tiers.name: Scythe-bearer
tiers.represents: Elite. The most capable opposition in the program
tiers.description: Boss-tier, and rarer than that. If one is here, you are no longer being handled by a process.

$ai_comment: Enemies wander; they do not home in. Canon gives the player the informational advantage - the program does not know where the intruder is - so noticeRadius is an encounter distance rather than a detection sweep: roughly a body length or two, not most of a screen. They amble between roam targets at wanderSpeed, notice the player only on getting close (or on being hit), pursue at speed, and forget after forgetSeconds once the player is past loseRadius. The player sees them coming; they do not see the player coming.
$weight_comment: How much of a shove an enemy absorbs: knockback is divided by it. A Scythe-bearer taking the same 46-unit slide as a goblin would make tier meaningless at exactly the moment it should be most legible.
